items: Petrochemical industry: produces plastics, synthetic rubber and fibres from crude oil. Crude oil is cracked (broken down) into smaller molecules, which become the building blocks for lubricants, waxes and synthetic rubbers.

Cosmetics industry: makes ingredients for make-up, soaps and perfumes. It uses surfactants (for soaps), emulsifiers (to keep creams smooth) and preservatives (to prevent bacterial growth); chemistry makes sure these products are pH-balanced for human skin.

Cement industry: uses limestone and clay to make a key building material. An intimate mixture of limestone and clay is heated to about 1500 C in a rotary kiln, and the product is ground with gypsum to make cement.

Food industry: makes food additives, preservatives and food-processing chemicals. Sodium benzoate is widely used as a preservative; hydrogenation turns edible oils into solid fats such as margarine; leavening agents such as sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) are used in baking; and foods are fortified by adding iodine to salt or vitamin A to oil.

blocks.alt: Four panels. Petrochemicals: crude oil is cracked into smaller molecules, the building blocks for plastics, rubber, fibres, lubricants and waxes. Cosmetics: surfactants, emulsifiers and preservatives; pH-balanced products. Cement: limestone and clay go into a rotary kiln at about 1500 C and the product is ground with gypsum; cement warms when mixed with water. Food: sodium benzoate preservative, hydrogenation of oils to margarine, baking soda, iodine in salt and vitamin A in oil.
blocks.caption: Applications of industrial chemistry (original diagram for topic 32.13).
blocks.long_description: The same chemical ideas, cracking, heating mixtures, hydrogenation and neutralisation, appear across very different industries.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Why does cement get hot when you add water? Cement reacts with water in an exothermic hydration reaction, releasing heat, which is why freshly mixed cement becomes warm.
